sentences.text: Ordered to give up the navy, Admiral Yi took his last thirteen ships to fight a hundred and thirty-three.
Even his own captains think he has lost his mind.
Korea's fleet has just been burned to the waterline by a Japanese invasion fleet.
So the king tells Yi to come ashore and fight on land.
Yi writes back, "I still have ships."
Then he anchors them at the mouth of the narrowest, loudest strait in Korea.
The locals call it the crying strait, for the roar of its water.
The Japanese fleet pours in with the current behind it, ship after ship, faster than any oar could row.
His captains hang back and politely let the admiral go first.
For hours, his flagship holds the front almost alone.
You see, the water in that strait runs like a river, and it turns around four times a day.
The Japanese had ridden the current into a gap so narrow only a few ships could reach him.
When the tide turned, historians reckon, that same current shoved their ships backwards into each other.
Korean records count ship after ship lost that day, and not one of his.
The king thought Yi had no navy left, but he had a sea that changes sides.
